tape.what: A steel blade on a spring reel, for measuring anything up to 16 feet.
parts: It slides in and out by exactly its own thickness on purpose, so a measurement is right whether you hook it over an edge or push it against a wall.
The thumb switch holds the blade out so it does not snap back while you mark.
The length of the case is printed on its base. For an inside measurement, push the case into the corner and add that number.
Each inch is split into sixteenths; the longest lines are halves, then quarters, eighths and sixteenths. Feet are marked every 12 inches.
The curve keeps the blade stiff so it can reach across a gap without drooping.
Holds the tape on a pocket or belt.
how: Hook the end over the edge, or push it flat against the surface.
Pull the blade straight and flat along what you are measuring, then lock it.
Read the mark looking straight down at it, and make a small V with the point on the measurement.
Guide the blade back in by hand.
watch: Letting the blade whip back can bend the hook and hurt fingers.
Do not hammer the loose hook tight. The movement is what keeps it accurate.

hammer.what: A claw hammer drives nails in and pulls them back out.
parts: The flat striking end. Hit the nail square with the middle of it.
The forked end slides under a nail head to lever it out.
Hold it near the end for power, closer to the head for small careful taps.
how: Hold the nail and tap it until it stands on its own, then move your fingers away.
Swing from the elbow and let the weight of the head do the work.
To pull a nail, slide the claw under the head and rock the handle back. A scrap of wood under the head protects the surface and adds leverage.
watch: Wear safety glasses. Nails and chips fly.
Never hit one hammer face with another; hardened steel can chip.

adjwrench.what: One wrench whose jaw opens and closes to fit many sizes of nut and bolt.
parts: The solid jaw that is part of the handle. It should take the force.
The worm wheel you roll to open or close the jaw.
Some have size marks on the head showing how far the jaw is open.
how: Put the jaws all the way onto the nut, then roll the thumb screw until there is no wobble.
Turn so you are pulling the handle toward the side with the moving jaw. That puts the force on the fixed jaw.
Tighten the jaw again each time you put the wrench back on.
watch: A loose jaw rounds off the corners of the nut.
Pull the handle toward you rather than pushing, so a slip does not send your knuckles into something.

diagonal.what: Cutters for snipping wire, zip ties and component legs close to a surface.
parts: The cutting edges run along one side, so you can cut flush.
Squeeze near the ends for the most force.
how: Put the wire deep in the jaws, close to the pivot.
Point the cut end away from faces, or cup it with your other hand.
Squeeze in one firm motion.
watch: They are for copper and soft wire. Steel wire, screws and nails notch the blades.
Never cut a wire that is powered.

linesman.what: Heavy flat-nosed pliers for gripping, twisting wires together and cutting.
parts: Grip and twist wires or hold flat parts.
The blades just behind the jaws cut wire.
how: Grip two stripped wires side by side at the tips and turn to twist them together.
Use the side cutter for the cut.
watch: Padded handles are for comfort. They do not protect you from electricity unless they are marked as insulated.

needlenose.what: Long thin pliers for reaching into small spaces, bending wire and holding tiny parts.
parts: Hold small parts and bend wire into loops.
Many have a small wire cutter near the pivot.
how: Hold small parts at the tips, and grip harder things further back near the pivot.
To make a loop, grip the wire end at the tip and roll your wrist.
watch: The tips bend if you twist hard or pry with them. Use heavier pliers for force.

slipjoint.what: General pliers with a pivot that moves between two positions, so the jaws can open wider.
parts: Open the handles fully and slide the pivot to the other hole for a wider jaw.
Grip round things like rods and pipes.
Some have a small wire cutter at the base of the jaws.
how: Pick the narrow or wide position before you grip.
Hold round things in the curved part.
watch: They round off nuts. Use a wrench or socket on anything you want to keep in good shape.

waterpump.what: Long-handled pliers with a jaw that slides through several grooves to grip large round things.
parts: Open the handles wide and move the jaw to another groove to change the size.
Grip pipes, large nuts and lids.
how: Choose the groove where the jaws sit almost parallel on the part with the handles a comfortable hand-width apart.
Turn in the direction that pushes the part toward the upper jaw, so the teeth bite.
watch: The teeth mark soft metal and plastic. Wrap the part in a cloth if the finish matters.

level.what: Shows whether something is truly flat or truly upright, and measures short lengths.
parts: One tube reads level (flat), one reads plumb (upright). Some have a third for 45 degrees.
Sticks to steel so you have both hands free.
Marked for measuring and for drawing straight lines.
how: Put the level on the surface and read the tube that lies along the direction you are checking.
It is level when the bubble sits exactly between the two lines.
To check the level itself, read it, turn it end for end on the same spot and read again. Both readings should match.
watch: Dirt under the edge changes the reading. Wipe the edge and the surface first.

benchsupply.what: Gives a steady, adjustable DC voltage for testing circuits, in place of batteries.
parts: Set how many volts come out. Many have a coarse and a fine knob.
Set the most current the supply will allow. This limit is what protects your circuit.
Shows the volts and the amps being drawn.
CV means it is holding the voltage you set. CC means your circuit hit the current limit and the voltage has dropped.
Red is positive, black is negative. A green post, if there is one, is earth ground and is not the negative.
On some models nothing comes out until you press it.
how: With nothing connected, set the voltage you need.
Turn the current limit down low, a little above what your circuit should draw.
Switch the output off, connect red to positive and black to negative, then switch it on.
Watch the amps. If the CC light comes on, switch off and find out why.
watch: Check the voltage before you connect. A knob that got bumped can destroy a 3.3 or 5 volt part instantly.
Reversing red and black can kill a circuit.

ratchetdriver.what: One handle with swappable tips, and a ratchet so you can turn screws without letting go.
parts: Three positions: tighten, loosen, and locked like an ordinary screwdriver.
A magnetic socket in the shaft that holds the tips.
Phillips (cross), slotted (flat), Torx (star), hex and square, each in several sizes.
Each bit is stamped, for example PH2 or T15.
how: Pick the bit that fills the screw head with no wobble. PH2 fits most common cross-head screws.
Push the bit into the holder and set the switch for the direction you want.
Push in firmly while you turn. Turn right to tighten, left to loosen.
Put every bit back in its slot before returning the set.
watch: A bit that is too small or the wrong type chews up the screw head.
Use the locked position to break a stuck screw free; the ratchet is for the easy turns.

socketset.what: A ratchet handle and a case of sockets for turning nuts and bolts quickly.
parts: Turns the socket one way and clicks freely the other, so you never take it off the nut.
The small lever on the head switches between tighten and loosen.
On many ratchets, press the button on the back of the head to drop the socket.
The square peg, usually 1/4 or 3/8 inch. A socket only fits the matching drive.
Two families: metric in millimetres and SAE in fractions of an inch. Deep sockets fit over long bolts.
Goes between ratchet and socket to reach recessed nuts.
how: Find the socket that slides on snugly. If it rattles, try the next size down or the other family.
Click it onto the ratchet and flip the lever for your direction.
Hold the head of the ratchet steady with one hand and swing the handle with the other.
Return every piece to its marked place in the case.
watch: A metric socket that almost fits an inch nut will round it off.
Do not slide a pipe over the handle for extra force. It breaks the ratchet.

f-buttonhole.what: Makes a whole buttonhole in one go, sized to your button.
parts: The sliding plate at the back. Put your button in it and push it closed; that sets the length.
Moves back and forth as the machine sews both sides and both ends.
A tab on the frame that the machine’s buttonhole lever rests against.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Choose the buttonhole stitch, and pull the machine’s buttonhole lever straight down so it sits behind the tab on the foot.
Mark where the buttonhole starts, lower the foot on the mark and sew. The machine stops by itself.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-buttonhole4.what: A clear foot for sewing a buttonhole in four steps, where you can see your marks through it.
parts: Lets you see the fabric marks.
Marks along the side for measuring the buttonhole length.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Mark the start and end of the buttonhole on the fabric.
Follow the buttonhole steps on the machine’s stitch dial in order: one side, the end bar, the other side, the last bar.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-blind.what: Sews a hem that barely shows on the outside.
parts: A thin blade in the middle that rides against the folded edge.
On many versions, moves the guide left or right so the needle just catches the fold.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Fold the hem up, then fold it back on itself so a small edge sticks out.
Choose the blind hem stitch and run the fold along the guide. The wide stitch should catch only a thread or two of the fold.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-button.what: Holds a flat button still while the machine sews it on.
parts: Clamp the button and leave the holes clear.
On many versions, stops the button sliding.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Lower or cover the feed dogs so the fabric does not move.
Choose a zigzag and set its width to the distance between the holes. Check by turning the handwheel by hand that the needle drops into each hole.
Sew about ten stitches, then tie off the threads on the back.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-embroidery.what: A foot for decorative and dense stitches.
parts: Lets you see the stitches as they form.
Gives thick satin stitching room to pass without jamming.
A foot with a spring and a small ring is for free-motion work, where you move the fabric by hand with the feed dogs lowered.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Put stabiliser or a second layer under thin fabric so it does not pucker.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-hemmer.what: Rolls the raw edge under twice and stitches it, making a very narrow hem.
parts: The curled funnel at the front that rolls the fabric edge.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Fold and press the first inch of the hem by hand, sew two or three stitches to hold it, then stop with the needle down.
Lift the foot, feed the fabric edge into the scroll, lower the foot and sew slowly, holding the edge slightly to the left so it keeps feeding in.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-overedge.what: Wraps stitches around a raw edge to stop it fraying.
parts: The wall on the right that the fabric edge runs along.
A thin wire in the middle that the stitch forms over, so the edge stays flat.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Choose an overcast or wide zigzag stitch.
Turn the handwheel by hand first to check the needle clears the pin on both swings.
Run the raw edge against the guide.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-walking.what: Has its own moving teeth on top, so the top layer and bottom layer feed at the same speed.
parts: Move the top layer in step with the machine’s teeth underneath.
The lever on the right that must sit over the needle clamp screw; the needle bar drives it.
An optional rod for evenly spaced quilting lines.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Take off the whole foot holder, not just the sole. Fit the walking foot with its fork arm resting on the needle clamp screw, then tighten the foot screw.
Use it for quilts, slippery or stretchy fabric, vinyl, and for matching stripes or plaids.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Sew at a steady medium speed, and mostly forward. Fast sewing and long reverse runs wear it out.
Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

f-zipper.what: A narrow foot that lets the needle sew right beside zipper teeth or piping.
parts: Presses on one side of the needle only.
Clip it on the left or right bar depending on which side of the zipper you are sewing.
how: Switch the machine off and raise the needle and the presser foot.
Take off the foot that is on. Snap-on feet drop off with the lever or button behind the holder; screw-on feet come off with the screw on the left.
Clip the foot on so it sits on the opposite side of the needle from the zipper teeth.
Use a straight stitch. Stop with the needle down, lift the foot and slide the zipper pull out of the way as you reach it.
Fit this foot, then turn the handwheel toward you by hand for one full stitch to be sure the needle misses the foot.
Test on a scrap of the same fabric first.
watch: Feet are made for a certain machine type. If it does not sit straight or the needle touches it, stop and ask at the desk.

bobbins.what: Small spools that hold the lower thread in a sewing machine.
parts: Wound with thread and dropped into the bobbin case under the needle plate.
Machines take one specific type. They look alike but differ in height and shape.
how: Compare a bobbin from this set with the one already in the machine. They must be the same height and shape.
Wind it on the machine’s winder until it is evenly full, and trim the tail.
Put it in so the thread comes off in the direction shown in the diagram by the bobbin case.
watch: The wrong bobbin type causes tangles and skipped stitches.
Do not wind new thread over old.

crochet.what: A hooked needle for looping yarn into fabric.
parts: The shaft sets the loop size, so its width is the hook size.
Printed on the flat grip in millimetres, sometimes with a letter.
how: Check the yarn label for the hook size it suggests.
Hold the hook like a pencil or a knife, whichever is comfortable, with the yarn over your other index finger.
Wrap the yarn over the hook and pull it through the loop.
watch: A hook much smaller than the yarn label suggests makes stiff, tight fabric; much larger makes it loose and holey.

ironingboard.what: A padded folding table for pressing.
parts: Under the board. Squeeze it to raise, lower or fold the legs.
The metal end or rack where a hot iron can stand.
Slide sleeves, trouser legs and shoulders over it.
how: Stand it on its end, squeeze the lever and pull the legs out until it locks at hip height.
Push down on it gently to be sure it has locked before putting an iron on it.
To fold, tip it on end, squeeze the lever and close the legs.
watch: Keep fingers clear of the legs when folding.
Let the cover cool and dry before folding it away.

pinking.what: Scissors with zigzag blades. The zigzag edge slows down fraying on woven fabric.
parts: Cut a zigzag instead of a straight line.
Fits several fingers for a strong, steady cut.
how: Cut with long, full strokes.
Line the teeth up with the last zigzag before each new cut so the pattern continues.
watch: Fabric only. Paper and tape dull the teeth quickly.
They do not help on knits and are not for cutting out pattern pieces accurately.

seamripper.what: A tiny forked blade for cutting stitches without cutting the fabric.
parts: The sharp part is the curve between the two prongs.
The short prong with a ball. It slides along the fabric without catching.
Covers the point; on many it also fits the back as a longer handle.
how: To remove a seam, slide the point under every third or fourth stitch and cut it, then pull the thread on the other side.
To open a seam fast, put the ball side between the two layers and push along the seam.
Pick out the cut threads.
watch: Push away from your body and your other hand.
Go slowly on thin fabric. It cuts fabric as easily as thread.

thimble.what: A hard cap that protects your finger when pushing a needle through fabric by hand.
parts: Catch the end of the needle so it does not slip.
how: Wear it on the middle finger of your sewing hand. It should stay on when you shake your hand, without squeezing.
Hold the needle between thumb and index finger and push the eye end with the side or tip of the thimble.
watch: It feels clumsy for the first few minutes. That passes.

textilekit.what: A kit of small hand tools for sewing and fabric work.
parts: Kits vary. Open it at the desk and check what is inside against the list in the case, if there is one.
how: Count the pieces when you borrow it and again before you return it.
Keep pins and needles in their holder so none are loose in the case.
watch: Fabric scissors are for fabric only. Cutting paper dulls them.

woolmat.what: A thick felted wool pad for pressing. It holds heat, so fabric is pressed from both sides at once.
parts: Grips fabric lightly so seams stay where you put them and come out flatter.
how: Lay it on a firm table or ironing board.
Press by lifting the iron and setting it down, not by sliding.
watch: Heat and steam pass through the mat. Protect a wooden or finished table underneath.
It can smell of wet wool when steamed. That is normal.
Store it flat, not folded.

iron.what: Presses creases out of fabric with heat and steam.
parts: Dots match the care label on clothes: one dot for synthetics, two for wool and silk, three for cotton and linen.
Turns steam off or sets how much comes out.
One mists water ahead of the iron; the other gives a strong shot of steam for stubborn creases.
Fill through the opening at the front, up to the MAX line.
The flat back end. Stand the iron on it whenever you put it down.
how: Fill the tank with the iron unplugged.
Check the care label on the fabric and set the dial to match. Start with the coolest fabrics.
Wait for the light to go off, which means it has reached temperature.
When finished, unplug it, empty the tank and let it cool standing on its heel.
watch: Steam only works on the two and three dot settings. Lower than that, water drips out.
Never leave it face down or unattended. Many irons switch off by themselves, but do not count on it.

iron-travel.what: A small iron for pressing on the go. It works like a full-size one with a smaller tank.
parts: Dots match the care label on clothes: one dot for synthetics, two for wool and silk, three for cotton and linen.
Turns steam off or sets how much comes out.
One mists water ahead of the iron; the other gives a strong shot of steam for stubborn creases.
Fill through the opening at the front, up to the MAX line.
The flat back end. Stand the iron on it whenever you put it down.
Some travel irons have a 120/240 switch. In the US it must be on 120.
On many, the handle folds flat for packing.
how: Fill the tank with the iron unplugged.
Set the dial to match the fabric care label and wait for it to heat.
Unplug, empty the tank and let it cool fully before folding it.
watch: The small tank runs out quickly. Refill unplugged.

steamer.what: Relaxes wrinkles with steam while the clothes hang. Nothing hot presses on the fabric.
parts: Fill to the line with the steamer unplugged.
Standing models have a hose and a pole to hang the garment on.
Starts the steam, which takes a minute or so to arrive.
how: Fill the tank and hang the garment.
Switch on and wait for steady steam.
Hold the fabric taut at the bottom and move the head slowly down it, lightly touching.
Unplug, let it cool and empty the tank.
watch: Steam burns. Keep your free hand below and away from the head, and never steam clothes someone is wearing.
Keep the head upright or it can spit hot water.

c-fine.what: Holds the fine-point blade, the everyday Cricut blade for paper, cardstock, vinyl and iron-on.
parts: The metal holder that goes in the machine.
A tiny replaceable blade held in by a magnet.
The button on top. Press it to push the blade out for changing.
how: Open clamp B on the machine, drop the housing in so its ridge sits on the clamp, and close the clamp.
Choose your material in Design Space; it sets the pressure for you.
To change the blade, press the plunger, pull the old blade out by its side and let the magnet take the new one.
watch: The blade is very sharp and very small. Change it over a table, not your lap.

c-deep.what: Holds the deep-point blade, which has a steeper angle for thicker materials such as chipboard, craft foam, magnet sheet and thick cardstock.
parts: Black so you can tell it apart. Deep-point blades only fit this housing.
Press the top to push the blade out for changing.
how: Put it in clamp B the same way as the normal blade.
Choose the exact material in Design Space. It will ask for the deep-point blade when one is needed.
Use the strong grip (purple) mat for heavy materials and tape the edges.
watch: Do not swap blades between the fine and deep housings.

c-rotary.what: A small rolling blade for cutting fabric and other soft materials without dragging them.
parts: The gold gear lets the machine steer the blade. It only works in Cricut Maker machines.
A 12 mm wheel that rolls through the material.
Stays on the blade end when not in use.
how: Put it in clamp B of a Maker with the gears meshing, and close the clamp.
Stick the fabric to the pink fabric mat.
Choose the fabric in Design Space and cut.
watch: It does not work in Explore or Joy machines.
Shapes smaller than about 3/4 inch can damage the mat and blade.

c-mat.what: The sticky sheet that holds your material flat while the machine cuts.
parts: The colour tells you: blue is light grip for paper, green is standard for cardstock and vinyl, purple is strong for thick materials, pink is for fabric.
Inch and centimetre lines that match the mat shown in Design Space.
Keeps dust off the glue. Put it back after every use.
how: Press the material onto the grid where Design Space shows it.
Slide the mat under the two guides and press the load button.
After cutting, turn the mat face down and peel the mat away from the material so the material stays flat.
watch: Do not touch the sticky side of the pink mat; skin oil ruins it.
Scrape off scraps after each job so the next one sticks.

c-pen.what: Lets the Cricut draw or write instead of cut.
parts: Printed on the barrel, for example 0.4 for fine.
Keep it. An uncapped pen dries out.
how: Open clamp A, take the cap off and push the pen down until it clicks, then close the clamp.
In Design Space, set the line to Draw (called Pen in newer versions) instead of Cut.
Take the pen out and cap it as soon as the job ends.
watch: The machine will not remind you to remove the pen.

c-tools.what: Hand tools for finishing Cricut projects.
parts: A hook for picking out the small unwanted pieces of vinyl or iron-on.
Rubs vinyl down firmly and cleans scraps off a mat.
Slides under delicate cuts to lift them off the mat.
For trimming material before and after.
how: Check which tools are in the set when you borrow it.
Weed with the vinyl still on its backing, starting from a corner.
watch: The weeder is sharp. Cap it or lay it flat.

c-scraper.what: A wide scraper for large Cricut projects.
parts: Covers more area in one pass than the small scraper.
how: Hold it at a low angle and rub firmly across vinyl to stick it down, working from the middle outward to push out bubbles.
To clean a mat, scrape scraps off in one direction.
watch: Do not scrape the pink fabric mat. Use tweezers on that one.

c-usb.what: Connects a Cricut machine to a computer when you are not using Bluetooth.
parts: Goes into the back of the Cricut.
Goes into the computer. A newer laptop may need a USB-C adapter.
how: Plug in both ends and switch the machine on.
Open Design Space; it should find the machine by itself.
watch: Newer machines such as Maker 3 and Joy may use a different cable. Check the port on the machine first.

cable-inst.what: Carries the sound from a guitar, bass or keyboard to an amp, pedal or audio interface.
parts: One black band on each plug: one mono, unbalanced signal.
A braid around the wire that keeps out hum.
how: Turn the amp or channel volume down.
Plug into the instrument first, then the amp or interface.
Turn the volume up slowly.
watch: Plugging in with the volume up makes a loud pop that can damage speakers.
Do not use it between an amplifier and a speaker cabinet. That job needs a speaker cable.
Coil it in loose loops; tight wrapping around your elbow breaks the wire inside.

cable-xlr.what: The standard microphone cable. It carries a balanced signal, which stays clean over long runs.
parts: Ground, signal and inverted signal. Noise picked up along the way cancels out.
The end with holes plugs into the microphone.
The end with pins plugs into the mixer, recorder or interface.
Clicks in. Press the tab to release.
how: Turn the channel down and switch phantom power off.
Plug into the microphone, then the mixer or interface.
If the mic is a condenser, switch phantom power (48V) on now, then bring the level up.
watch: Pull by the plug while pressing the latch, never by the wire.
Plug and unplug with phantom power off to avoid a loud thump.

cable-xlr-trs.what: Joins XLR gear to 1/4 inch gear, for example a mixer output to a powered speaker.
parts: Male (pins) sends into an input; female (holes) accepts a microphone or an output.
how: Check which way the signal needs to flow, and that the XLR end is the right sex for the socket you are going into.
Turn levels down, connect, then bring levels up.
watch: A microphone plugged into a 1/4 inch line input this way will be very quiet, and it gets no phantom power.

cable-aux.what: The small stereo cable for joining a phone, laptop or player to a speaker, mixer or recorder.
parts: Count the black bands on the plug. One band (TS) is a single mono signal. Two bands (TRS) is either stereo or one balanced mono signal. Three bands (TRRS) adds a microphone, as on phone headsets.
The large plug used on guitars, keyboards, mixers and studio headphones.
The small plug used on phones, laptops and ordinary headphones.
how: Plug one end into the headphone or line output and the other into the input marked AUX or LINE IN.
Start with the source volume at about three quarters and set loudness on the speaker or mixer.
watch: A cable with three bands (TRRS) can give thin or one-sided sound in a plain stereo socket. Use one with two bands.

adapt-jack.what: Changes the size of a headphone or line plug so it fits a different socket.
parts: Count the black bands on the plug. One band (TS) is a single mono signal. Two bands (TRS) is either stereo or one balanced mono signal. Three bands (TRRS) adds a microphone, as on phone headsets.
The large plug used on guitars, keyboards, mixers and studio headphones.
The small plug used on phones, laptops and ordinary headphones.
how: Look at the socket you need to fit and the plug you have.
Push the plug fully into the adapter until it clicks, then plug the adapter in.
watch: A half-seated plug gives sound in one ear only.
The weight of an adapter can strain a small socket. Support the cable.

cable-rca.what: Carries left and right audio on two separate plugs, to gear such as turntables, DJ mixers, older stereos and TVs.
parts: If there is one, it is for video, not sound.
how: Match the colours at both ends.
Push each plug fully on; they are a tight fit.
watch: RCA is unbalanced, so keep runs short and away from power cables to avoid hum.

cable-dmx.what: Joins a 3-pin XLR socket to a 5-pin DMX socket on stage lighting gear.
parts: The standard DMX connector on controllers and professional lights.
Many smaller lights use this for DMX, even though it looks like a microphone socket.
how: Run from the controller’s DMX OUT to the first light’s DMX IN, then OUT to IN down the chain.
Set a DMX address on each light.
watch: It is for lighting control. Do not join audio gear to lighting gear with it.

cable-midi.what: Carries note and control messages between keyboards, synths, drum machines and interfaces. It carries no sound.
parts: Each cable sends one way only.
how: Connect MIDI OUT on the device you play to MIDI IN on the device that should respond.
For two-way talk, use a second cable the other way.
Set both to the same MIDI channel.
watch: OUT to OUT does nothing. If nothing responds, check OUT goes to IN.

splitter.what: Splits one headphone or line socket into two.
parts: Each takes headphones or a cable.
how: Plug it into the output, then plug both sets of headphones in.
watch: Both listeners share the same volume, and it gets a little quieter for each.
Some splitters are for a headset: one socket for headphones, one for a microphone. Look for the icons.

usb-audio.what: A tiny sound card. It gives a computer or phone a headphone socket through its USB port.
parts: Goes into the computer, tablet or phone.
For headphones or a cable to speakers. Some also take a headset microphone.
how: Plug it in and wait a few seconds.
Choose it as the sound output in the computer’s sound settings.
Plug in the headphones.
watch: If there is no sound, the computer is probably still sending to its own speakers. Check the output setting.

dpa.what: Lets a DPA miniature microphone, which ends in a tiny screw-on MicroDot plug, connect to other gear.
parts: Either XLR for a mixer or recorder, or a plug for a wireless bodypack.
how: Screw the MicroDot connection finger-tight.
For the XLR type, plug into a mic input and switch on 48V phantom power; the adapter needs it.
For the wireless type, plug into the matching bodypack and lock the ring.
watch: The MicroDot thread is delicate. Never use pliers.
Wireless adapters are made for one brand of transmitter. Check the label.

hdmi.what: Carries picture and sound from a laptop, camera or player to a screen or projector.
parts: Standard (TVs, projectors, laptops), Mini (some cameras and tablets) and Micro (small cameras, some action cams). They are not interchangeable.
how: Check the socket size on both devices.
Plug in both ends, then choose the matching HDMI input on the screen.
On a laptop, choose whether to mirror or extend the display in display settings.
watch: The plug only goes in one way. Do not force it.
If sound still comes from the laptop, choose the screen as the sound output.

hdmi-split.what: Sends one HDMI source to two screens showing the same thing.
parts: Most need their power adapter plugged in to work.
how: Connect the source to IN and each screen to an OUT.
Plug in the power.
Switch the screens on first, then the source.
watch: It copies one picture. It cannot extend a desktop across two screens.
Both screens get the resolution the weaker one can handle.

hdmi-dvi.what: Joins HDMI gear to a DVI monitor or projector.
parts: The wide white plug with two thumbscrews.
Plug or socket, depending on the adapter.
how: Connect and tighten the thumbscrews by hand.
Choose the DVI input on the screen.
watch: DVI carries no sound. Send audio separately.

minidp.what: Connects a computer with a Mini DisplayPort or Thunderbolt 2 socket, such as an older MacBook or a Surface, to a screen.
parts: Small, with one flat side and two angled corners. It is the same shape as Thunderbolt 2.
The type of screen it reaches: HDMI, DVI, VGA or DisplayPort.
how: Plug the small end into the computer and the other end into the screen or its cable.
Choose the matching input on the screen.
watch: These adapters work one way: computer out to screen. They will not connect an HDMI device to a Mini DisplayPort monitor.
It does not fit USB-C.
VGA carries no sound.

thunderbolt.what: A fast link for drives, docks and screens on computers with Thunderbolt.
parts: Use the USB-C shaped plug, marked with a lightning bolt.
Use the Mini DisplayPort shaped plug, also marked with a lightning bolt.
how: Check the lightning bolt mark on the computer’s socket.
Plug in both ends. Drives and docks appear by themselves.
watch: A USB-C socket without the lightning bolt is not Thunderbolt, and Thunderbolt-only devices will not work in it.

usb.what: Connects a device to a computer or charger for data, power or both.
parts: The flat rectangle found on most computers and chargers.
The square plug used on printers, audio interfaces and Arduino Uno and Mega boards.
Small plugs on older phones, cameras and many Arduino-type boards. Micro is thin and flat; Mini is thicker.
The small oval that goes in either way up.
A blue tab in a USB-A plug or socket usually means USB 3, which is faster.
how: Match the plug at each end to the sockets on your two devices.
Plug in. Most devices show up by themselves.
watch: Some cables only carry power. If a device charges but the computer cannot see it, try another cable.
Not every USB-C cable carries video or fast data, even though the plug is the same.

usb-adapt.what: Lets a plug of one USB shape fit a socket of another.
parts: The flat rectangle found on most computers and chargers.
The square plug used on printers, audio interfaces and Arduino Uno and Mega boards.
Small plugs on older phones, cameras and many Arduino-type boards. Micro is thin and flat; Mini is thicker.
The small oval that goes in either way up.
A blue tab in a USB-A plug or socket usually means USB 3, which is faster.
how: Check which side is the plug and which is the socket.
Fit the adapter to the cable or device first, then plug it into the computer.
watch: It changes the shape only. It does not make a slow port fast or add video.

usbc-video.what: Sends the picture from a USB-C laptop, tablet or phone to an HDMI screen.
how: Plug into the computer, then connect the HDMI side to the screen.
Choose the HDMI input on the screen.
watch: The USB-C port must support video out. Look for a DisplayPort or Thunderbolt symbol beside it, or check the device’s specs. Many phones and cheaper laptops do not.

usbc-eth.what: Gives a laptop without a network socket a wired internet connection.
parts: Takes a network cable. Its small lights blink when it is connected.
how: Plug it into the computer, then click a network cable into it and into the wall or router.
Wait a few seconds for the connection.
watch: On campus, a wired device may need to be registered on the network before it gets online.

lightning-hdmi.what: Shows an iPhone or iPad screen on a TV or projector.
parts: Goes into the iPhone or iPad.
For the cable to the screen.
For a charger, so the device stays powered while showing.
how: Plug the adapter into the device and an HDMI cable into the adapter and screen.
Choose the HDMI input on the screen. The device’s screen is mirrored.
watch: It only fits devices with a Lightning port, not USB-C ones.
Some streaming apps block playback through it.

hub.what: Turns one USB port into several, and on USB-C models adds sockets a thin laptop lacks.
parts: For drives, keyboards, mice and so on.
USB-C hubs often add HDMI, SD and microSD slots, Ethernet and a charging-in port marked PD.
how: Plug the hub into the computer first, then devices into the hub.
If it has a PD port, plug the laptop charger in there to keep charging.
watch: Everything shares one port’s power. Hard drives and audio interfaces may misbehave; plug those straight into the computer.
Eject drives before unplugging the hub.

ethernet.what: A network cable for a wired internet or device connection.
parts: The tab on the plug clicks in. Press it to release.
Printed on the cable: Cat5e, Cat6 and so on. Any of them handles ordinary use.
how: Push each end in until it clicks.
Look for the small lights by the socket to confirm a link.
watch: A broken clip lets the plug slide out. Report it.
Some audio and lighting gear uses the same plug for something that is not a network. Only join gear that is meant to be joined.

parts: The round one is the ground. Never bend or break it off.
Printed on the cord in amps or watts.
how: Uncoil it fully.
Plug the cord into the wall first, then the device into the cord.
Tape it down or route it along a wall where people walk.
watch: Do not chain cords or power strips together.
A cord left coiled can overheat under a heavy load such as a heater or large light.

powerstrip.what: Turns one wall outlet into several.
parts: Usually lit. It also acts as a breaker and may pop off if overloaded.
All share the one wall outlet’s capacity.
how: Plug it into a wall outlet and switch it on.
Spread large plugs so they do not block neighbours.
watch: Do not plug one strip into another.
Heaters, kettles and irons belong in a wall outlet, not a strip.

usbpower.what: A wall plug with a USB socket, for charging or powering small devices.
parts: Printed in small type: volts and amps. 5V at 1A is slow; 2A or more is faster.
how: Plug a USB cable into it and the device, then plug it into the wall.
watch: A device that needs more current than the plug can give will charge slowly or restart.

aa.what: Reusable AA cells for microphones, flashes, controllers and other gear.
parts: Rechargeable AAs are NiMH and give 1.2 volts, a little less than the 1.5 of throwaway ones. Nearly all gear is fine with that.
The plus end has the raised button.
how: Match plus and minus to the marks in the battery door.
Use cells from the same set together.
Bring them back whether or not they are flat; staff recharge them.
watch: Do not mix them with ordinary batteries in one device.
Never put them in a charger that is not made for NiMH.

sd.what: Storage for cameras, recorders and computers.
parts: On the left edge of a full-size card. Slid down, the card cannot be written to or erased.
A number in a U or after a V shows how fast it records. U3 or V30 handles 4K video.
The fingernail-size version. An adapter sleeve lets it fit a full-size slot.
how: Copy off anything on it that you need.
Put it in the camera or recorder and use that device’s Format command. This erases the card and sets it up correctly.
When done, copy your files off and eject the card on the computer before pulling it out.
watch: Formatting erases everything.
If the camera says the card is locked, check the switch on the edge.
Your files are not private once you return it. Delete them.

reader.what: Lets a computer read a memory card.
parts: Full-size SD and usually microSD. Multi-card readers add older types such as CompactFlash.
how: Plug the reader into the computer.
Slide the card in, label facing the way the icon shows, until it stops.
Copy your files, then eject the card on the computer before pulling it out.
watch: Pulling a card out mid-copy can corrupt it.

parts: Usually small button cells or AAAs under the end cap.
how: Point at the screen, then press.
Rest your hand on something to keep the dot steady.
watch: Never point it at anyone’s eyes, at vehicles or at aircraft.
It will not show on most TV-type screens as well as it does on a projected image.

wagon.what: A folding cart for moving gear across campus.
how: Undo the strap and pull the sides apart until the base lies flat. Press the base board down if it has one.
Put heavy things at the bottom and over the wheels.
To fold, empty it, pull up on the loop in the middle of the base and push the sides together.
watch: Keep fingers out of the frame as it folds.
Pull it, do not ride in it, and take ramps rather than stairs.

mic.what: Turns sound into a signal for a recorder, mixer or audio interface.
parts: Cardioid hears mostly what is in front and rejects the back. Omnidirectional hears all round. Shotgun hears a narrow beam straight ahead.
A dynamic mic needs no power. A condenser needs 48V phantom power from the mixer or recorder, or its own battery.
Most use a 3-pin XLR. Small clip-on mics use a thin plug made for a wireless pack.
Some have an on/off or a low-cut switch on the body. Check it first if you get no sound.
how: Turn the channel gain down, connect the mic, and switch on phantom power only if it is a condenser.
Speak or play at the real volume and raise the gain until the meter sits mostly green, with peaks just touching yellow.
Listen on headphones before you record anything that matters.
watch: Red on the meter means it is distorting, and that cannot be fixed afterwards. Turn the gain down.
Do not blow into a mic or tap it to test it. Talk.

mic-wireless.what: A microphone that sends its sound by radio to a receiver, so there is no cable between the person and the mixer or camera.
parts: The handheld mic itself, or a small pack worn on a belt with a clip-on mic plugged into it.
The box that plugs into the mixer, recorder, camera or phone.
Transmitter and receiver must be on the same channel, or paired. Two-channel systems have a separate channel for each mic.
Usually separate. A muted mic stays connected.
Transmitters run on AAs or a built-in battery. Check the level on the display before every use.
how: Put in fresh or fully charged batteries.
Switch on the receiver first, then the transmitter, and check they link: a light or the display on the receiver shows a signal.
Connect the receiver output to your mixer, recorder or camera and set the level as for any microphone.
Walk the area you will use while someone listens for dropouts.
watch: Keep the receiver where it can see the transmitter. Bodies and walls block the signal.
Switch transmitters off before returning them so batteries are not drained.

boompole.what: A telescoping pole that holds a microphone over the people talking, just outside the camera’s view.
parts: Slide out and lock with a twist collar each.
A 3/8 inch screw for a mic clip or shock mount.
Padded so your hands make less noise.
how: Mount the mic and wrap the cable loosely round the pole so it cannot slap.
Extend the thickest sections first and leave a hand-width of each inside for strength.
Hold it above your head with arms wide, mic pointing down at the speaker’s chest from in front.
Watch the camera screen for the mic or its shadow dipping into the shot.
watch: Do not slide your hands along the pole while recording; the mic hears it.
Look up for lights and ceiling fittings before raising it.

hpamp.what: Splits one headphone signal to several pairs of headphones, each with its own volume.
parts: From the headphone or line output of a mixer, interface or computer.
how: Turn all the knobs down.
Connect the source to the input and plug in the headphones.
Bring each knob up to a comfortable level.
watch: Start low every time. Sudden loud sound in headphones can hurt.

micclip.what: Holds a handheld microphone on a stand.
parts: The mic slides or snaps in.
Screws onto the stand. US stands use 5/8 inch; a small brass insert adapts to the 3/8 inch thread on European stands and boompoles.
how: Screw the clip onto the stand first.
Slide the mic in from the front, cable end first, then angle it.
watch: Clips are sized for a mic’s body. A thin mic falls out of a wide clip.

popfilter.what: A mesh screen between your mouth and a microphone. It stops the bursts of air from P and B sounds from thumping.
how: Clamp it to the stand, not the mic.
Place the screen two or three fingers in front of the mic.
Sing or speak about a hand-width back from the screen.
watch: It does not reduce room noise or echo.

dibox.what: If the label says Pyle PDC21, this is a direct box. It lets a guitar, bass or keyboard plug into a microphone input on a mixer over a long cable without hum.
parts: Passes the same signal on to an amp.
Goes to a mic input on the mixer with a normal mic cable.
If you hear a steady hum, flip it.
If it has one, it turns a loud source down.
how: Instrument cable into the input, mic cable from the XLR output to the mixer.
Bring up the mixer gain as you would for a mic.
watch: Check the label on the item before relying on this; the inventory name is only a part number.

sustain.what: A foot pedal for a keyboard. Notes ring on while it is held down, like the right pedal on a piano.
parts: Goes into the socket marked SUSTAIN or DAMPER on the keyboard.
Many pedals have a small switch underneath, because keyboard brands wire them opposite ways.
how: Plug it in before switching the keyboard on, and keep your foot off it as the keyboard starts.
Play and press. Notes should hold only while the pedal is down.
watch: If it works backwards, flip the polarity switch or restart the keyboard with your foot off the pedal.

headphones.what: Closed studio headphones for listening while you record, edit or mix.
parts: Usually the small 3.5 mm plug with a screw-on or push-on 1/4 inch adapter for mixers and interfaces.
Marked inside the headband or on the cups.
how: Turn the volume down before you put them on.
Check left and right are the right way round.
Bring the volume up to where you can still hear someone talk to you.
watch: Keep the 1/4 inch adapter with the headphones when you return them. It is the part that goes missing.
If you hear one side only, push the plug fully in.

cassette.what: Plays, and on many models records, cassette tapes.
parts: Play, stop/eject, fast forward, rewind, and record if it has it.
Also the way to send sound to a computer or speaker with an aux cable.
AA batteries or a power adapter.
how: Open the door and put the tape in with the open edge toward the heads, the side you want facing out.
Close the door and press play.
To copy a tape to a computer, run an aux cable from the headphone socket to the computer’s line input and record there.
watch: Fully stop the tape before pressing a different button.
Pressing record erases what is on the tape.

ecello.what: A cello with a pickup instead of a hollow body. It is nearly silent until you plug it in.
parts: 1/4 inch, for an amp, interface or headphones if it has a headphone socket.
Many have a 9V battery for the built-in preamp.
The spike at the bottom and the knee or chest rests that stand in for a cello body.
how: Set the end pin and fit the rests so it sits like a normal cello.
Tighten and rosin the bow, tune the strings (C G D A, low to high).
Turn the amp down, plug in with an instrument cable, then bring the volume up.
watch: Loosen the bow before putting it away.
Unplug the cable when finished; on many, leaving it plugged in drains the battery.

micromoog.what: A 1970s Moog analog synthesizer. It plays one note at a time and you shape the sound with knobs.
parts: Makes the raw tone. Its waveshape knob sweeps from sawtooth to square to narrow pulse.
Cutoff removes brightness; emphasis adds a whistling peak. This is the Moog sound.
Set how fast the sound starts and dies away, for loudness and for the filter.
The strip left of the keys bends pitch as you slide a finger on it.
1/4 inch on the back, a low and a high level. It has no speaker.
how: Turn the amp or interface down, connect an instrument cable from the output, and switch on.
Let it warm up for several minutes; the pitch drifts until it does.
Start with the filter cutoff about halfway and the emphasis low, then change one knob at a time and listen.
watch: It has no MIDI, no USB and no memory. Take a photo of the knobs to save a sound.
It is old and hard to replace. Turn knobs gently and carry it flat.

midictl.what: A controller with pads, knobs or faders that sends MIDI messages to music software over USB. It makes no sound itself.
parts: Carries power and data on one cable.
Hit harder for louder. Usually used for drums and triggering clips.
Each can be assigned to a control in your software.
how: Plug it into the computer; no power adapter is needed.
Open your music software and switch the controller on in its MIDI settings.
Load an instrument or drum kit on a track, arm the track, and play.
watch: No sound usually means no instrument is loaded, or the controller is not enabled in the software’s MIDI settings.

footpedal.what: A pedal that plugs into a computer by USB so your foot can trigger something while your hands are busy.
parts: Powers it and sends the signal.
how: Plug it in and press a pedal with a text document open to see what it sends.
Many of these act like a keyboard key and can be set to a different key with the maker’s software.
watch: Check the label for the maker and model; setup differs between them.

mixer.what: Combines microphones and instruments, lets you balance and shape each one, and sends the result to speakers or a recorder.
parts: Each input has one column of controls, top to bottom: gain, EQ, sends, pan, mute and fader.
Sets how much the input is boosted. Set this first.
A button that removes rumble. Use it on voices.
High, mid and low knobs. Straight up is neutral.
Send some of a channel to stage monitors or to the built-in effects such as reverb.
Places the channel left or right.
The level of that channel in the mix.
The overall level to the speakers.
One switch that powers condenser mics.
Sends the mix to a computer for recording and plays computer sound back.
how: Pull all faders down and turn gains down. Connect everything, then switch on the mixer first and the speakers last.
Bring the main fader up to the 0 or U mark.
For each channel: have the person play or talk, raise the gain until the level lights are mostly green, then bring up that fader.
Switch off in reverse: speakers first, then the mixer.
watch: Red clip lights mean turn the gain down, not the fader.
A squeal is feedback. Pull the fader down, then move the mic behind the speakers or away from them.

soundblanket.what: A heavy quilted blanket that soaks up echo so recordings sound less like a bare room.
parts: Metal rings along one edge on many, for hanging.
how: Hang it behind and beside the person speaking, or over a stand or a door.
Lay another on a hard floor or table under the mic.
watch: It reduces echo inside the room. It does not stop noise coming through walls.
Keep it off hot lights.

speaker.what: A speaker with its own amplifier. Plug in a sound source and power, and it plays.
parts: A 3.5 mm aux socket, RCA, 1/4 inch or USB, depending on the model.
On the front, side or cable.
A wall adapter, or USB on small ones.
how: Turn the volume right down.
Connect power and the cable from your source, then switch on.
Start your sound and bring the volume up.
watch: Plugging or unplugging a cable with the volume up makes a loud bang.

partybox.what: A large portable Bluetooth speaker for events.
parts: Hold it until it flashes, then pick the speaker on your phone.
A 3.5 mm socket on the back for a cable.
Some models have 1/4 inch sockets with their own volume.
Turns the light show on or off.
A button that adds low end.
Wall power, and on some models a built-in battery.
how: Plug it in or check the battery, and switch on.
Pair your phone, or connect an aux cable.
Set your phone to about three quarters and control loudness on the speaker.
watch: It is heavy. Lift with two hands by the handles.
Hunt Library is a quiet building. Test it somewhere it is welcome.

micstand.what: Holds a microphone at the right height and angle.
parts: Three folding legs, or a heavy round plate.
The collar you twist to raise or lower the upright.
On many, a second arm that swings out, with its own lock.
5/8 inch at the top for a mic clip.
how: Spread the legs all the way.
Set the height, then tighten the clutch.
If it has a boom, point the arm over one of the legs so it cannot tip.
Screw on the clip and add the mic last.
watch: Loosen locks before moving anything. Forcing a tight joint strips it.
Take the mic off before folding the stand.

speakerstand.what: A tripod that lifts a PA speaker above head height so sound carries over a crowd.
parts: Spread wide and lock with a knob.
Telescopes, with a locking knob and a safety pin through a hole.
A 1 3/8 inch (35 mm) pole that fits the socket under most PA speakers.
how: Spread the legs until the braces are nearly flat.
Raise the pole, put the safety pin through, and tighten the knob.
Lift the speaker on with two people, and lower the socket onto the pole.
watch: Always use the pin. The knob alone can slip.
Keep cables taped down so no one pulls the stand over.

lightstand.what: A folding stand that holds a light, reflector or backdrop up high.
parts: Fold out from the bottom. Wider is steadier.
Telescope and lock with a knob or lever each.
A 5/8 inch pin that a light slides over and clamps to. Many also have a 1/4 or 3/8 inch screw on the tip.
how: Spread the legs fully and lock them.
Mount the light at chest height and tighten its clamp on the stud.
Raise the top, thinnest section last, and lock each one firmly.
Lower it one section at a time, holding the section as you loosen its lock.
watch: Put a weight or sandbag on a leg when the stand is tall or outdoors.
Point one leg in the direction the light leans.
Run the cable down the stand and tape it where people walk.

backdrop.what: Two stands and a crossbar that hold a roll of paper or a cloth backdrop behind your subject.
parts: Comes in sections that slot together; fewer sections make it narrower.
The crossbar ends drop over the pins and are held by wing nuts.
Hold cloth tight and stop a paper roll unwinding.
how: Set up both stands low, legs wide.
Join the crossbar and slide it through the paper roll or the pocket in the cloth.
Drop the bar onto both pins and fit the wing nuts.
Raise both stands a little at a time, one side then the other, keeping the bar level.
watch: Two people make this much easier and safer.
Weigh the legs down. A backdrop acts like a sail.

keyboard.what: A wired keyboard for a computer, tablet or a board such as a Raspberry Pi.
parts: Works as soon as it is plugged in.
Show Caps Lock and Num Lock.
how: Plug it in and wait a few seconds.
On a Mac, a window may ask you to press the key next to Shift so it can tell the layout.
watch: On a Mac, the Windows key acts as Command and Alt as Option.

parts: USB-A or USB-C. Check which your computer has.
Scrolls, and clicks as a third button.
The light underneath that reads movement.
how: Plug it in. It works within a few seconds.
Use it on a plain, non-shiny surface.
watch: It will not track on glass or a mirror-like desk. Put a sheet of paper under it.

opticaldrive.what: Plugs into a computer by USB to read discs, and usually to burn them.
parts: Where the disc goes, label side up.
A straightened paperclip pushed in here opens a stuck tray with the power off.
Some have two plugs; the second is for extra power.
how: Plug it straight into the computer, not through a hub.
Press eject, click the disc onto the spindle, and close the tray.
The disc appears on the computer after a few seconds.
watch: If the drive clicks or will not spin, it is short of power. Use both USB plugs or a different port.

monitor.what: A 27 inch screen for a laptop or desktop.
parts: On the underside at the back: usually HDMI and DisplayPort, and on some models USB-C.
On the lower right edge or the back. They open the menu for input, brightness and so on.
Most Dell stands tilt, raise and lower, and turn the screen upright. A button on the back releases the stand.
Work only if the monitor’s USB cable is also connected to the computer.
how: Connect power and one video cable, then switch on.
If it says No Signal, open the menu and choose the input your cable is in.
In the computer’s display settings choose mirror or extend, and drag the screens to match how they sit on the desk.
watch: Carry it by the frame and stand with two hands. Do not press on the screen.

webcam.what: A camera that plugs into a computer for video calls, streaming and recording.
parts: Folds to sit on top of a screen. Many also have a tripod thread underneath.
Shows when the camera is on.
A sliding lens cover on some.
how: Clip it to the top of the screen and plug in the USB cable.
In your call or recording app, pick it as the camera, and as the microphone if you want.
Put your main light in front of you, not behind.
watch: If the picture is black, check for a privacy shutter and that no other app is using the camera.

3dglasses.what: Powered glasses for watching 3D from a projector. Each lens flickers dark in time with the picture so each eye sees its own image.
parts: A coin cell or a USB-charged battery.
On the front, between the lenses on many.
how: Put the projector into its 3D mode and play 3D material.
Switch the glasses on and look at the screen; they lock on in a few seconds.
If the depth looks wrong or uncomfortable, use the projector’s 3D invert or sync setting.
watch: They only work with a projector that uses the same 3D system. Borrow them together with the projector they belong to.
Without 3D material playing, the picture just looks dim.

phonemount.what: A spring clamp that holds a phone on a tripod, stand or light.
parts: Pull the jaws apart; they spring back onto the phone.
A 1/4 inch hole underneath fits any tripod screw.
Some turn between upright and sideways, and some have a shoe on top for a small light or mic.
how: Screw the mount onto the tripod first.
Open the clamp and seat the phone in the middle, clear of the side buttons.
Give it a gentle shake before letting go.
watch: A thick case may not fit. Take it off rather than forcing the clamp.

tubelight.what: A stick-shaped LED light with a built-in battery, for colour accents, backgrounds and handheld lighting.
parts: Steps between white light, colours and moving effects.
Buttons or a dial, with a small display.
A tripod thread at the end, and on many a magnet in the body.
how: Charge it fully before a shoot.
Hold the power button to switch on, pick a mode, then set brightness and colour.
Place it just out of shot, or in shot as a glowing line.
watch: Full brightness drains the battery much faster.
The magnets are strong; keep it away from cards and hard drives.

ledkit.what: LED panel lights with stands, for lighting people and sets for photo and video.
parts: On two-colour lights, from warm orange (about 3200K, matches indoor bulbs) to cool blue-white (about 5600K, matches daylight).
A white panel or cloth that softens the light.
A wall adapter, and on many a plate on the back for camera-style batteries.
The U-shaped bracket that tilts the light and clamps onto a stand.
how: Set up the stands, mount each light at about chest height and tighten, then raise.
Set every light to the same colour temperature, and set your camera’s white balance to match.
Start with one light in front of the subject, off to one side and a little above eye level. Add a second, dimmer one on the other side to soften shadows.
Let lights cool before packing.
watch: Mixed colour temperatures make skin look odd. Match them.
Count the parts back into the bag: lights, stands, adapters, diffusers.

gels.what: Thin coloured or frosted sheets that go in front of a light to change its colour or soften it.
parts: Tint the light for mood or effect.
Makes a daylight-coloured light match warm indoor bulbs.
Makes a warm light match daylight.
how: Clip the gel to the light’s barn doors or frame with wooden clothespins or clips, leaving an air gap.
Set your camera’s white balance before adding colour gels, or the camera will cancel the colour out.
watch: Hot lights melt gels. Keep them off the lamp and lens, and leave space for air. LED lights run much cooler.
Do not cut the sheets without asking.

screen.what: A portable white screen for a projector.
parts: The tube that the screen rolls into.
A hook on the upright that holds the top of the screen.
Set how high the case and the top sit.
how: Open the legs fully.
Turn the case so it is level, then pull the screen up by its handle and hook it on the hanger.
Raise the upright until the screen is tight and at the height you want.
To pack up, lower it, unhook, and guide the screen back in by hand.
watch: Do not let the screen snap back into the case.
Keep fingers and pens off the surface; marks show in every picture.

cam360.what: A camera with two or more very wide lenses that records everything around it at once.
parts: Bulging glass on opposite sides. They are the easiest part to scratch.
The maker’s phone app shows a live view and changes settings.
how: Charge it and put in a card.
Mount it on a thin stand or pole at head height; a 360 camera sees whatever is holding it.
Start recording, then step away or accept that you are in the shot.
Copy the files off and join the lens images in the maker’s app or desktop software if the camera does not do it by itself.
watch: Things closer than about an arm’s length show a visible seam.
Never lay it on its side. Use the pouch.
Older 360 cameras may no longer have a working phone app. Check at the desk before planning a project around one.

reflector.what: A folding disc that bounces or softens light. One disc with a zip-on cover gives five surfaces.
parts: The bare inner disc. Hold it between the sun or a light and your subject to soften harsh light.
how: Unzip the cover and turn it to the side you want.
Hold it opposite the main light and tilt until you see the shadows on the face lift.
To fold: grip opposite edges, twist your hands in opposite directions and let it collapse into three rings.
watch: It catches wind. Hold on.
Silver and gold can dazzle. Check your subject is comfortable.

lensadapter.what: Lets a Sony A-mount lens fit a Sony E-mount camera.
parts: The larger opening, with a release button for the lens.
Fits the camera like a lens.
Match the dots, then turn until it clicks.
how: Switch the camera off.
Fit the adapter to the camera, then the lens to the adapter.
Switch on and check focus and aperture work.
watch: Autofocus depends on which adapter this is and which lens. Test before a shoot.
Keep caps on both ends when it is off the camera.

bracket.what: A metal frame or bar that holds a camera together with extras such as a light, microphone or second camera.
parts: A 1/4 inch screw that goes into the tripod hole on the camera.
Extra threaded holes or shoes for accessories.
Underneath, so the whole thing goes on a tripod.
how: Screw the camera on firmly.
Add accessories and balance the weight so it does not tip forward.
watch: Finger-tight plus a little. Over-tightening damages the camera’s thread.

canonbatt.what: A rechargeable battery for Canon Vixia camcorders that take the BP-7 series.
parts: The metal end goes in first.
It clicks in; a release switch on the camcorder lets it out.
how: Slide it into the battery slot on the back until it clicks.
To charge, leave it in the camcorder, plug the camcorder’s power adapter in and switch the camcorder off. The light shows charging.
watch: There is no separate charger: it charges inside the camcorder.
Borrow it with the camcorder it fits.

canonpower.what: The wall power adapter for the Canon Vixia HF R800 camcorder.
parts: Goes into the DC IN socket on the camcorder.
how: Plug it into the camcorder and the wall to run the camcorder for as long as you like.
With the camcorder switched off, it charges the battery inside.
watch: It is made for this camcorder family. Do not use it on other gear.

dummybatt.what: Runs a Canon camera from the wall, in place of its LP-E6 type battery, for long recordings, time-lapses and streaming.
parts: A battery-shaped block with a cord, which goes in the battery slot.
A small rubber flap on the camera’s battery door that lets the cord out so the door can close.
Plugs into the wall and into the dummy battery cord.
how: Switch the camera off and take out its battery.
Slide in the dummy battery, lead the cord through the flap and close the door.
Connect the adapter, plug it into the wall and switch on.
watch: If the plug is pulled, the camera loses power instantly and may lose the clip it was recording.
Check it fits your camera model before borrowing.

camfan.what: A small fan that attaches to the back of a camera to stop it overheating during long video recording.
parts: Blows across the back of the camera body.
Clips or sticks on behind the flip-out screen.
From a power bank or wall plug.
how: Fold the camera’s screen out of the way and fit the fan to the back of the body.
Plug in USB power and switch on before you start recording.
watch: The microphone on the camera may pick up the fan. Use a separate mic.

magicarm.what: A jointed arm that holds a small light, monitor, camera or flag exactly where you want it.
parts: Joined by an elbow, with a ball joint at each end.
One control frees or locks all the joints together.
A 5/8 inch stud or a 1/4 inch screw at each end.
Grips a pole, table edge or pipe, and has a socket the arm fits into.
how: Fix the clamp to something solid and tighten it hard.
Loosen the arm, attach your item, and hold the item with one hand the whole time.
Move it into place and lock the arm before letting go.
watch: When you unlock it, everything goes limp at once. Always hold the load first.
Keep to light loads, a few pounds at most, and less when the arm is stretched out sideways.

dvd.what: Plays DVD video discs on a TV or projector.
parts: HDMI on newer players. Older ones have three round sockets: yellow for picture, red and white for sound.
Needed for disc menus on many players.
how: Connect it to the screen and choose that input on the screen.
Load the disc and use the remote to pick Play from the menu.
watch: Check the remote is with it, and has batteries, before you leave the desk.
It will not play Blu-ray discs.

dragonframe.what: A USB keypad for the Dragonframe stop-motion program, so you can shoot and review frames without going back to the computer keyboard.
parts: Play back what you have shot or step through one frame at a time.
Switches between the live camera view and the frames you have taken.
how: Plug it into a computer that has Dragonframe installed and a camera connected.
Open your scene, then use the keypad from wherever you are animating.
watch: It does nothing without the Dragonframe program. Check which campus computers have it.

slider.what: A short rail that a camera glides along, for smooth sideways or push-in moves.
parts: The sliding block. It has a screw on top for a camera or tripod head.
A knob that locks the carriage. Some also have a drag knob for resistance.
Adjustable legs at each end for uneven ground.
Under the middle and often each end.
how: Lock the brake, then mount the slider on a tripod or stand it on its feet, and level it.
Fit a tripod head to the carriage and the camera to that.
Release the brake and push from the carriage, not the camera, with steady pressure.
watch: Lock the brake before you carry or tilt it, or the camera slides off the end.
On one tripod, a long slider tips as the camera reaches the end. Support both ends.

tripod.what: Holds a camera steady and at a fixed height.
parts: Each has two or three sections with a flip or twist lock.
Raises the camera a little more. Use it last; it is the least steady part.
Tilts and turns the camera. A handle or knobs lock it.
A small plate that screws into the bottom of the camera and clips into the head.
Shows when the head is level.
how: Take the plate off the head and screw it into the camera with a coin.
Extend the thickest leg sections first and spread the legs fully.
Level it by adjusting leg lengths, then clip the camera in and check the latch has closed.
Loosen a lock before moving that part, and tighten it again after.
watch: Keep a hand on the camera until you have checked the plate is locked.
Return the plate with the tripod. Without it the tripod is useless to the next person.

minitripod.what: A pocket-size tripod for a table top, for a small camera, phone mount, light or microphone.
parts: Fold out, and on some extend.
A 1/4 inch screw fits any camera, phone mount or small light.
On some, a ball with a locking knob for aiming.
how: Spread the legs fully on a flat surface.
Screw the camera or phone mount on, then aim and lock.
Folded, the legs make a hand grip.
watch: It tips with a heavy camera or a long lens. Keep the weight over the middle.

gorillapod.what: A small tripod with bendable legs that can stand on rough ground or wrap around a railing, branch or pole.
parts: Each ball joint bends. Rubber rings grip.
Aims the camera and locks with a knob.
On some, a small plate that stays on the camera.
how: To stand it, bend the legs outward so the feet are wide.
To wrap it, wind all three legs tightly round the object, then tug the camera to test it.
Aim with the ball head and lock it.
watch: Keep within the weight it is made for. When wrapped, keep a hand or strap on the camera.

lens.what: A lens for a camera with interchangeable lenses.
parts: The metal ring that locks into the camera. A lens only fits cameras with the same mount.
A small number is a wide view; a large number is a close, narrow view. Two numbers mean it zooms.
The widest the opening goes. A smaller number lets in more light and blurs backgrounds more.
Turn it to focus by hand.
On zoom lenses, the wider ring.
On autofocus lenses, switches between automatic and hand focus.
Front and rear caps protect the glass; the hood blocks stray light and takes knocks.
how: Switch the camera off and point it downward.
Take off the body cap and the rear lens cap, match the dot on the lens to the dot on the mount, and turn until it clicks.
To remove it, hold the release button on the camera and turn the other way. Put both caps back on straight away.
watch: Check the mount matches your camera before borrowing.
Do not touch the glass or leave the camera open without a lens or cap.
Clean only with a blower and lens cloth.

wmr.what: A Windows Mixed Reality headset. It plugs into a Windows PC and tracks its own position with the cameras on its front, so there are no sensors to set up in the room.
parts: Ends in two plugs: HDMI (or DisplayPort on some) and USB 3.
Track the room and the controllers. Do not cover them.
Two, each on two AA batteries, paired by Bluetooth.
A dial or strap tightens it; on most the visor flips up.
how: Check with staff which computer this headset still works with before planning around it.
Plug both plugs straight into the PC. The Mixed Reality Portal should open and walk you through setup.
Pair the controllers and trace the edge of your clear space when asked.
Adjust the band so the weight sits on your forehead, and the picture is sharp.
watch: Microsoft has removed Windows Mixed Reality from current versions of Windows 11. These headsets only run on a PC that still has an older version.
They track poorly in dim rooms.
Clear the floor and keep the cable behind you.

rift.what: A PC virtual reality headset. A gaming-class Windows PC does the work and the headset is its display.
parts: HDMI and USB on the original Rift; DisplayPort and USB on the Rift S.
The original Rift comes with two or more small desk sensors that plug into USB 3 and watch the headset. The Rift S has cameras on the headset instead.
A slider under the original Rift sets the distance between the lenses.
how: Install the Meta Quest Link app (once called the Oculus app) on the PC and follow its setup.
Plug the headset, and any sensors, straight into the PC’s graphics card and USB 3 ports.
Place sensors about two metres apart, pointing at where you will stand, then draw your play boundary.
Tighten the straps so the picture is sharp and the weight is off your nose.
watch: It needs a PC with a dedicated graphics card. Most laptops cannot run it.
Meta has stopped selling Rift headsets, and new software may not support them. Test early.
Clear the floor around you.

1/4\" Audio Cable: Check the plugs: one band is an instrument cable, two bands is a balanced or stereo cable.
1/4\" AUX Extension: One end is a socket, so it makes another 1/4 inch cable or headphone lead longer.
3-Pin XLR Adapter: A short piece that changes a plug to a socket or the other way round, so two ends that would not meet can join. Check which ends it has.
1/8\" to 1/4\" AUX: Small plug on one end, large on the other. Good for a phone or laptop into a mixer or instrument amp input.
1/8\" to 1/4\" Adapter: Small plug on one end, large on the other.
1/4\" to 1/8\" Adapter: Check which side is the socket: that is the size of plug it accepts.
Check which side is the socket: that is the size of plug it accepts.
1/8\" to 1/4\" Audio Adapter: Usually lets ordinary small-plug headphones fit a large socket on a mixer, interface or keyboard.
1/8\" to RCA: One small stereo plug splitting into red and white. For a phone or laptop into a stereo, mixer or powered speakers.
RCA Cable, 1/8\" (Audio): One small stereo plug splitting into red and white.
3.5mm to 2-Male RCA Adapter: One small stereo socket or plug splitting into red and white.
RCA to 1/4\" Adapter: Lets an RCA cable plug into a 1/4 inch socket, or the reverse. Check which side is which.
5-Pin XLR Adapter: A 5-pin connector is used for DMX lighting control. Check which ends the adapter has.
HDMI Cable 40ft: A long run. Some long cables have a chip in one end and only work one way round: look for ends marked Source and Display. Test before your event.
MiniHDMI: Mini plug on one end, as used on many cameras.
HDMI F-F Ext: A coupler with two sockets that joins two HDMI cables into one longer one. Very long joined runs may lose the picture.
HDMI 90 F-M: A right-angle piece for plugging in where there is no room behind a screen.
HDMI(in) to 2xDVI: Takes one HDMI source and feeds two DVI screens.
Mini DisplayPort to DVI: Mini DisplayPort plug on the computer side.
DisplayPort to HDMI: Full-size DisplayPort plug on the computer side.
HDMI (out) to VGA: Takes HDMI from a computer and feeds an older VGA screen or projector. VGA carries no sound; some of these have a small audio socket for that.
Thunderbolt 3 to Thunderbolt 2 Adapter: Joins Thunderbolt 3 (USB-C shape) and Thunderbolt 2 (Mini DisplayPort shape) gear in either direction. It does not pass power to a device and does not work with plain Mini DisplayPort screens.
Apple USB C-C Cable - 2m: USB-C at both ends. Apple’s charge cable carries power and slow data; it does not carry video.
USB 3.0 Cable: Check the ends: USB 3 plugs are often blue inside.
USB A to USB B Cable: The printer-style cable. Also used by many audio interfaces, MIDI keyboards and Arduino Uno and Mega boards.
USB A to USB B Micro: Micro plug on the device end.
USB A to USB B Mini: Mini plug on the device end.
USB C to A Cable: USB-C on one end, USB-A on the other.
USB Extension Cable: Plug on one end, socket on the other, to make a USB cable reach further. Very long runs can make devices drop out.
Lightning to USB A Adapter Cable: Lightning end for an iPhone or iPad with that port.
USB Memory Stick: A USB drive plugs straight into a computer; there is no lock switch or speed mark. Always eject it before unplugging.
Audio-Technica Cardioid Condenser Bounda: A flat mic that lies on a table, floor or wall and hears the half of the room above it. Good for meetings, stage floors and group conversation. It is a condenser, so it needs phantom power. Put it on a firm surface and do not cover it.
Audio-Technica Condenser Shotgun Microph: A long thin mic that hears mainly where it is pointed, for dialogue and video. Aim it at the mouth from just outside the picture, on a boompole or camera. It needs phantom power, or on some models an AA battery inside the body.
Beyerdynamic M-58 Omnidirectional Microp: A dynamic interview mic that hears all round, so it forgives being pointed loosely between two people. It needs no power and handles wind and handling noise well.
CAD 22 Handheld Cardioid Microphone: A dynamic handheld mic for voice. No power needed. Hold it by the body, two or three fingers from your mouth, pointed at your mouth.
CAI B3 LAVALIER: A very small clip-on mic that hears all round. Clip it about a hand-width below the chin and hide the cable inside clothing. Its plug is wired for one brand of wireless pack or for an XLR power adapter; check which before you borrow it.
Korg Microphone: Check the body for the model and for a switch.
Shure Microphone: Most Shure handheld mics are dynamic cardioids for voice, and need no power. Check the model printed on the body.
USB Mic: Plugs straight into a computer with a USB cable; no interface or phantom power needed. Choose it as the input in your recording app. If it has a headphone socket, plug in there to hear yourself with no delay.
Sony Omni Wireless Lavalier Microphone: A clip-on mic that hears all round, worn about a hand-width below the chin.
